name: Chiropractic neck adjustment

card.summary: High-velocity neck manipulation sometimes sought for posture and jaw or face alignment; case reports link it to arterial injury and stroke.
card.note: Case reports describe vertebral artery dissection and other serious complications after neck manipulation.

quick.overview:
A chiropractic neck adjustment is a thrust applied to the joints of the neck, usually by a chiropractor. In looksmaxxing and related fringe circles it is sometimes discussed as a way to correct posture or alignment thought to affect the face.

Research on cervical manipulation concerns neck pain, not appearance, and its safety is debated. Published case reports describe stroke and eye bleeding after neck manipulation.
quick.mechanism: A quick, small-amplitude thrust is applied to a cervical joint, often producing a popping sound. Practitioners say it restores joint movement. Reviewers describe the evidence for effect as limited and the degree of serious risk as uncertain.
quick.risks: The main concern is vertebral artery dissection, which can lead to stroke. A 2001 study reported higher rates of vertebrobasilar stroke in adults under 45 who had recently visited a chiropractor, with no significant association over 45. Some chiropractors dispute a causal link.

lead: A chiropractic neck adjustment, or cervical spinal manipulation, is a quick, small-amplitude thrust applied to the joints of the neck, usually by a chiropractor, osteopath or physiotherapist. Practitioners use it for neck pain, stiffness and cervicogenic headache, and some people in appearance communities seek it out in the hope of improving head and neck posture, which they associate with a straighter profile, a tidier jawline and a better-aligned look.

The posture-to-looks chain is a claimed one: proponents describe freer neck movement as supporting better head position, and head position is widely discussed as influencing how the jaw, chin and neck read in profile. No study has tested neck manipulation for facial appearance. The published research concerns pain and function. A 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence for spinal manipulation in neck pain, while some lower-quality evidence suggests multiple sessions may improve pain and function compared with some medications [1].
Safety is the most discussed topic in the literature. Vertebral artery dissection and stroke are the main reported serious harms, and reviewers say their frequency is uncertain [1][3][4].

paras: Cervical manipulation is usually a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust, often accompanied by an audible pop. It is widely used by physiotherapists, chiropractors, osteopaths and doctors for neck pain and cervicogenic headache [5]. A related literature tests manipulation of the upper cervical spine in people with temporomandibular disorder, a jaw pain condition, usually combined with other treatments [6].

A 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence for spinal manipulation in neck pain, and a 2007 review reported moderate-to-high-quality evidence of benefit for chronic neck pain not caused by whiplash [1]. A multicentre randomised trial in 120 people with temporomandibular disorder compared dry needling plus upper cervical manipulation with splint therapy, diclofenac and joint mobilisation [6]. Effects on facial or postural appearance have not been studied.

Reviewers describe little evidence of harm and little evidence of safety, and note that under-reporting is likely substantial [1]. A 2001 Stroke study found vertebrobasilar accidents were five times more likely in adults under 45 who had visited a chiropractor in the preceding week, with no significant association above 45; some chiropractors dispute that manipulation causes these events [1].

A 2013 systematic review of case reports found 43 articles describing 901 cervical artery dissections and 707 strokes reported in association with manipulation, and assessed the quality of those reports [3]. A 2017 systematic review of 144 studies covering 227 adverse-event cases found that cervical artery dissection was reported in 57 percent of them and that screening tests for at-risk patients appear unreliable [2]. A 2024 meta-analysis of randomised trials notes that the link between manipulation and serious events rests mostly on case-control studies and case reports, which cannot establish incidence or causation [5].

Individual case reports describe cerebellar infarction after a chiropractor's neck manipulation [7], preretinal haemorrhages after high-velocity cervical manipulation [8], and a fatal vertebral artery dissection in a woman who performed manipulation on herself [4].

No studies found on neck adjustment for facial appearance. Trials of cervical manipulation address neck pain, jaw disorders and short-term physiological measures, and the safety literature consists largely of case reports and reviews [1][5][6][7][8].

angle.text: Some people book neck adjustments hoping to correct forward head posture and alignment that they believe softens the jaw and neck line. The appearance effect is claimed by proponents and has not been studied.
